methods.label: Pair the opposite vertices
methods.explanation:
Every specified line contains the same center digit, so their sums are equal exactly when the four opposite vertex pairs have equal sums. Let \(j\) be the digit at \(J\), and let \(s\) be this common pair sum. Since all nine digits sum to \(45\),
\[
4s=45-j.
\]
Thus \(45-j\) must be a multiple of \(4\). Because \(1\le j\le9\), it lies between \(36\) and \(44\). The multiples of \(4\) in that interval are \(36,40,44\), giving exactly the center possibilities \(j=9,5,1\).

For each center digit, the opposite pairs are forced: a digit \(x\) must be paired with \(s-x\). The three cases give
\[
\begin{aligned}
j=1:&\quad (2,9),(3,8),(4,7),(5,6),\\
j=5:&\quad (1,9),(2,8),(3,7),(4,6),\\
j=9:&\quad (1,8),(2,7),(3,6),(4,5).
\end{aligned}
\]
Each list uses every remaining digit once and has the required common pair sum, so all three center choices work.

For a fixed center, assign the four pairs to the labeled positions \(AE,BF,CG,DH\). There are \(4\cdot3\cdot2\cdot1=24\) ways. Each pair can then be placed in either order at its two vertices, giving \(2\cdot2\cdot2\cdot2=16\) possibilities.

Every constructed assignment satisfies the line sums. Conversely, any valid assignment uniquely determines its center, the pair in each position, and each pair's order, so none is omitted or counted twice. The vertex labels distinguish assignments obtained by rotating or reflecting the digits. Therefore the total is
\[
3\cdot24\cdot16=\boxed{1152},
\]
which is choice \(\mathrm{C}\).
